newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends mixed in U.S., G7 officials endorse Rubin.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends mixed in U.S., G7 officials endorse Rubin.

text.p: The dollar ended mixed against key currencies but not far from new multi-year peaks reached after officials from Japan and France said the G7 was aligned with the U.S. position favoring a strong dollar, experts said.

Dollar/yen reached 119.20, a 46-month high, and dollar/mark set a 31-month peak at 1.6455 in Europe after Japan's Finance Minister and the head of France's central bank said the Group of Seven (G7) nations backed U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's exchange rate policy.
But the dollar's early advance was stymied by a fall in the U.S. stock market and remarks by a German central banker.

The dollar succumbed to mild profit-taking while U.S. stocks and bonds fell sharply. The Dow Jones stock average was down almost 34 points in late trade Wednesday, partially offsetting Tuesday's 40 point advance.
"When stocks go down, they try to push (the dollar) lower, but in the end I think the dollar against Europe is going higher," said Jeffrey Yu, senior dealer at Sanwa Bank Ltd.

The dollar ended at 118.90/00 yen, up from 118.75/85 at the open. It fell to 1.6400/10 marks from 1.6410/15. The dollar also set a 32-month high at 1.4360 Swiss francs, before closing at 1.4288/93 francs, down from 1.4315/25 at the open.
Comments from Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke also weighed on the dollar after he told journalists in Frankfurt the mark's slide could not continue "at the pace at which it had been going."

However, Welteke also said the weak mark posed no threat to the German economy or its stable inflation rate. By the close of trade, the dollar had overcome his mild warnings about the weak mark, reclaiming levels above 1.64 marks after hitting a low of 1.6335 marks in early U.S. dealings.
"He's talking out both sides of his mouth," said John Gariano, a vice president at Sumitomo Bank in New York.
"He's talking out both sides of his mouth," said John Gariano, a vice president at Sumitomo Bank in New York.
"Even though it's going to fuel some of their overseas export growth ... some of their import stuff is going to be higher in price now due to the fact the dollar is getting stonger," Gariano said.
The earlier G7 statements in support of the dollar came after Rubin restated his well-known preference for a strong dollar on Tuesday.
"The United States is calling the shots now," Yu of Sanwa Bank said.

"European central banks are very happy the dollar is higher. Japan, in the beginning, was worried about weakness of yen translating to weaker Nikkei stocks, but it seems like everybody is thinking differently now," Yu added.
Investors interpreted a comment from Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka as a signal to buy dollar/yen.

Although he said excessive yen strength or weakness was undesirable, Mitsuzuka also said "The U.S. has been saying that it is seeking a stong dollar. My understanding is that the G7 nations share that stance."
Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet expressed similar sentiments on the part of the G7 in a newspaper article, which boosted the dollar against the mark, dealers said.
Elsewhere, the surging dollar pushed the pound down to $1.6360/65 at the close from $1.6560/70 at the open.
The dollar closed at Canadian $1.3375/80, off from C$1.3379/84.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7756/61, up from $0.7752/57.
